title: Age-restricted sales and Challenge 25
siteNotes: The venue's age verification policy: whether it is Challenge 21 or Challenge 25, and where the written policy is displayed
Where the refusals log is kept and how to fill it in
Whether digital ID is accepted here (see legalNotes: this is changing)
Whether 16 and 17 year olds may drink beer, wine or cider with a table meal here, and any premises licence conditions on children
What to do with a suspected fake ID (who to tell, where it is kept) and who to call
Update the written age verification policy if the venue decides to accept digital ID (registered digital verification service only); until then the physical-ID teaching applies.
legalNotes: It is an offence to sell alcohol to a person under 18: Licensing Act 2003 s.146 (legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2003/17/section/146). Verified. A defence exists if the seller believed the person was 18 or over and took all reasonable steps to establish age (for example, asked for evidence that would have convinced a reasonable person), or nobody could reasonably have suspected they were under 18.

Mandatory age verification condition: Licensing Act 2003 (Mandatory Licensing Conditions) Order 2010, legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2010/860, paragraph 4 of the Schedule. Verified: the policy must apply to anyone who appears under 18 (or an older age set in the policy), and ID must show a photograph, date of birth and a holographic mark. Challenge 25 is not mandated; it is the usual way of meeting the condition.

Acceptable ID: a photocard driving licence, a passport and a card with the PASS hologram are accepted forms (Home Office guidance, assets.publishing.service.gov.uk). Military ID is accepted by many policies but was not verified against the guidance: flagged, so the session tells staff to follow the venue's policy.

Persistently selling alcohol to children: s.147A, two or more different occasions within three consecutive months. Verified. A penalty is a fine; the amount is not quoted because the page did not state it.
Allowing sales to children (s.147) is named in the licence record but its wording was not checked here: described only in general terms.

16 and 17 year olds: s.150 permits consumption of beer, wine or cider at a table meal on relevant premises when accompanied at the meal by someone aged 18 or over. Verified on legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2003/17/section/150. That an adult must buy the drink comes from secondary sources (Drinkaware) and was not verified in statute: flagged.

Proxy sales (an adult buying for a minor) are an offence for the adult under the Licensing Act 2003; the section number was not verified and is not quoted. Good practice is to refuse where you suspect it.

Digital ID: a government blog (June 2026) says new legislation removes the physical-hologram barrier for digital age checks in England and Wales. Details were not fully verified. The session teaches physical ID and tells staff to follow the venue's policy.
Other age-restricted goods (tobacco, vapes, knives) are outside what was checked and are not taught here.

Review 6 Oct 2026 corrections: (1) The mandatory age verification condition is paragraph 3 of the Schedule to the 2010 Order (legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2010/860), not paragraph 4 as first recorded; paragraph 4 is the small-measures condition. (2) The condition requires ID bearing a photograph, date of birth and EITHER a holographic mark OR an ultraviolet feature; slides and the check on the condition's wording were amended from 'hologram' only. (3) Digital ID: the Licensing Act 2003 (Mandatory Licensing Conditions) (Amendment) Order 2026, in force 15 September 2026 (approved by both Houses on 8 September 2026), lets a premises' policy accept digital proof of age verified through a registered Digital Verification Service (the register under s.32 Data (Use and Access) Act 2025, at least medium confidence). It is optional: premises may keep to physical ID, and passports and photocard driving licences remain valid. Source: the amended Schedule on legislation.gov.uk and law firm and trade summaries; the Order itself was not read in full. The phone-photo card was reworded to say a photo or screenshot of ID is not accepted. (4) s.146, s.147A (persistent selling: two or more different occasions within three consecutive months) and the table meal exception in s.149(5) and s.150 (16 or 17 year old, beer, wine or cider, at a table meal on relevant premises, accompanied at the meal by someone aged 18 or over) re-verified on legislation.gov.uk. The adult buying the drink is covered by s.149(5), now verified. (5) Slide 1 callout softened: not asking does not automatically remove a defence under s.146 (belief the person was 18 plus all reasonable steps, or nobody could reasonably have suspected from appearance), but in practice it almost always will. (6) The refusals log is good practice and often a licence condition, not a statutory requirement on its own; the session only says it shows reasonable steps, which is fair.

Not verified: PASS card named in Home Office s.182 guidance (summaries only); military ID; the Order's exact digital wording. GM or Ward Hadaway to confirm the venue's written policy states whether digital ID is accepted.

cards.kicker: Front of house, bar and events · 12 minutes
cards.title: Age-restricted sales and Challenge 25
cards.body:
By the end of this session you can:
- explain the law on selling alcohol to under-18s
- check ID properly and refuse safely
- record a refusal and spot a proxy sale

cards.title: Under 18: no alcohol sales
cards.body:
It is an offence to sell alcohol to anyone under 18 (Licensing Act 2003, s.146). A defence is possible if you took all reasonable steps to check their age, which usually means you asked for proper ID.

> If you did not ask for proof of age and they were under 18, you will almost certainly have no defence.

items.label: Minimum age to be sold alcohol
Sales in 3 months can make it 'persistent'

cards.title: Challenge 25
cards.body:
Every licensed venue must have an age verification policy. Ours asks for ID from anyone who looks under 25. Your manager will show you the written policy and whether it is Challenge 21 or 25.

The point is to give you a safe margin when ages are hard to judge.

items.title: Check
items.text: Photo, date of birth, security mark

cards.title: Which ID counts
cards.body:
ID must show a photo, a date of birth and either a hologram or an ultraviolet feature. Accepted examples are a passport, a photocard driving licence and a card with the PASS hologram. Follow the venue's policy on anything else, such as military ID.

From 15 September 2026 a venue's policy may also accept digital ID, but only if it is checked through a registered digital verification service. Photos and screenshots of ID do not count. Your manager will show you whether we accept digital ID.

Look at the photo, the date of birth and the hologram or UV mark, and check it is the person in front of you.

items.title: Photo on a phone
items.text: A photo or screenshot of ID is not accepted

cards.title: No ID, or ID you doubt
cards.body:
No ID means no sale. Stay polite and do not argue. If you think ID is fake or belongs to someone else, do not accept it and tell your manager. Do not snatch it or make accusations.

Your manager will show you what to do with suspected fakes.

left.title: Do
items: Tell your manager about a fake

cards.title: Buying for someone underage
cards.body:
Watch for an adult buying drinks and passing them to a younger person. If you suspect it, refuse the sale and tell your manager.

It can happen in the beer garden, at a wedding or at a table. Ask yourself who the drink is really for.

cards.title: The meal exception
cards.body:
16 and 17 year olds may drink beer, wine or cider with a table meal if accompanied by someone aged 18 or over. Not spirits, and not at the bar. Your manager will show you whether the premises allows it.

> We do not sell them alcohol; the adult buys it.

visual.yAxis: With an adult at a table meal?

cards.title: Refusals log and persistent selling
cards.body:
Log every refusal: date, time, what was asked for and a short description. Your manager will show you the log. It shows we take reasonable steps.

Selling to children on two or more occasions within three months can be an offence of persistently selling (s.147A).

cards.title: Remember
cards.body:
- Never sell alcohol to anyone under 18.
- Challenge anyone who looks under 25 and check photo, date of birth and hologram or UV mark.
- No ID, no sale. Stay polite.
- Watch for proxy buying and log every refusal.
- 16 and 17 year olds: only beer, wine or cider with a table meal and an adult.

cards.q: A young-looking guest orders a gin and tonic and says they left their ID at home but are definitely over 25. What do you do?
options: Serve it; they say they are over 25
Ask a friend to vouch for them
Refuse politely and offer a soft drink
Serve a single measure
cards.why: No ID means no sale. Vouching or a verbal promise does not count as proof.

cards.q: A 17-year-old with their parents can order their own pint at the bar.
cards.why: The only exception is drinking beer, wine or cider with a table meal when an adult is with them. We do not sell alcohol to under-18s.

cards.q: Which ID shows a photo, a date of birth and a hologram, as the policy needs?
options: A screenshot of a passport
A loyalty card with a photo
A card with the PASS hologram
A student card without a date of birth
cards.why: A card with the PASS hologram carries all three. A phone picture or a card without the right features does not meet the condition.

cards.q: Which TWO are signs of a possible proxy sale?
options: Two adults ordering a round
An adult buys drinks and hands them to a teenager
A guest asking for water
A nervous buyer glancing at younger friends
A family ordering lunch
cards.why: Passing drinks to someone younger, or an anxious buyer ordering for a younger group, are classic signs. Refuse and tell your manager.

cards.q: Writing a refusal in the refusals log helps show that the venue takes reasonable steps.
cards.why: The log is evidence that staff check age and refuse when they should, which matters if the venue is ever challenged.

cards.q: A guest looks about 22 and has no ID. Our policy is Challenge 25. What do you do?
options: Ask their age and trust what they say
Ask for ID; refuse if none
Serve them one drink only this time
Ask their friend to confirm the age
cards.why: Anyone who looks under 25 must be asked for ID. No ID means no sale.

cards.q: Under the age verification condition, acceptable physical ID must show a photograph, date of birth and a hologram or ultraviolet feature.
cards.why: That is the wording of the mandatory condition (a hologram or a UV feature). A passport, a photocard driving licence and a PASS card are examples.

cards.q: A man buys three pints and hands one to a lad of about 15 at the next table. What should you do?
options: Nothing, as the man is an adult
Refuse his next sale and tell a manager
Ask the lad his age and carry on serving
Tell the man off loudly in front of others
cards.why: This looks like a proxy sale. Refuse and tell your manager, without a scene.

cards.q: A 16-year-old at a table meal with an adult may be served a gin and tonic.
cards.why: Only beer, wine or cider with a table meal, when accompanied by an adult. Never spirits.

cards.q: Why is it important to log refusals?
options: It is a legal requirement for each drink served
It shows reasonable steps and reveals patterns
It lets us name and shame the person
It replaces the need for checking ID
cards.why: The refusals log is evidence that staff check age and refuse when they should, and managers can review it for patterns.
